Judy Heumann, widely regarded in that role, and learning more of her, even more than I ever imagined and heard about, she really was at the forefront in the major disability rights demonstrations. She helped spearhead the passage of the disability rights legislation.

She founded national and international disability advocacy organizations, and she held senior federal government positions. In the 1970s, Judy attended Camp Henned, a summer camp for people with disabilities in the Catskills, and she later returned there as a counselor.

Several of the leaders of the disability rights movement also were from Camp Henned, which was the focus of the documentary Crip Camp. But during the same decade, the New York Board of Education refused to give Judy a teaching license because they feared she could not help evacuate students or herself in the case of a fire.

She sued, and she went on to become the first teacher in the state to use a wheelchair. Continuing her fight for civil rights, Judy helped lead a protest that shut down traffic in Manhattan against Richard Nixon's veto of the 1972 Rehabilitation Act.

She launched a 26-day sit-in at the Federal Building in San Francisco to get Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act enforced. Judy was instrumental in developing and implementing national disability rights legislation, including Section 504, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

In addition, and this I was less aware of, she helped found the Berkeley Center for Independent Living, the Independent Living Movement, and the World Institute on Disability. She also served on the boards of many institutions and many across the board.

Judy moved to D.C. in 1993 to serve as the Assistant Secretary of the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitation Services in the Clinton Administration, a role she filled until 2001. She was also the first advisor on disability and development at the World Bank.

She worked as special advisor for international disability rights to the U.S. State Department, and she was appointed as D.C.'s first director of the Department on Disability Services. As Judy said, some people say that what I did changed the world, but really I simply refused to accept what I was told about who I could be, and I was willing to make a fuss about it.

As Judy mentioned, a president with polio could serve in the presidency, but she could not serve as a teacher and really led the fight for disability rights. So in honor of everyone in the community, we've lost a champion, and to her loving family, we send our thoughts and prayers.

Whereas multiple sclerosis, MS, is a neurological disease of the central nervous system, affecting nearly 1 million people in the United States alone, and generally strikes people in the prime of life between ages 20 through 50. research. And whereas while the cause and course of the often debilitating symptoms of MS remain unknown and no cure currently exists, the National MS Society is committed to a world free of MS, heightening public knowledge and insight into the disease. in the treatment of MS.
